In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This paper addresses circuit dysfunction in autism. In doing so, it nicely integrates computational (in silico) modelling with novel methods for the analysis of time series data, picking up on a recent thread on excitation-inhibition balance in neocortex. One very unique approach of the paper is the notion of a "behavioral camouflage" – that is, the ability mask social communicative difficulties through cognitive strategies: the authors find that a relatively intact E:I balance in medial prefrontal cortex may assist women with autism to recruit behavioural camouflage. This work obviously needs to be further nuanced with the various contributions of social gender roles, learning and cognitive strategies more broadly, as these pertain to persons with autism. This paper makes valuable contributions towards neurophysiological mechanisms of large-scale neurophysiological signals, the role of biophysical models in neuroscience, and our understanding of autism spectrum disorders.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Intrinsic excitation-inhibition imbalance affects medial prefrontal cortex differently in autistic men versus women" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Christian Büchel as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Takamitsu Watanabe (Reviewer #1); Richard Gao (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, we are asking editors to accept without delay manuscripts, like yours, that they judge can stand as eLife papers without additional data, even if they feel that they would make the manuscript stronger. Thus the revisions requested below only address clarity and presentation.

Summary:

This paper presents an impressive integration of in silico modelling, in-vivo rodent fMRI with chemogenetic manipulation and human fMRI. A number of key insights are advanced and integrated: the emerging and informative knowledge of time scale hierarchies in the brain; neurobiological and social aspects of autism spectrum disorder, including sex/gender considerations; and the role of computational models in linking micro- and macroscopic scales of investigation.

Revisions:

All three reviewers were impressed with the ambition and technical accuracy of the study. Their detailed technical suggestions are included below – all of which essentially request edits to the text (mainly Introduction and Discussion), more detailed appraisals of the data, and further visualizations. There are no new data acquisitions required and the additional analyses are suggested to improve the depth and quality of the presentation.

Reviewer 2 challenges the link between BOLD and LFPs versus spiking behaviour. Since the work of Logothetis and colleagues (and as confirmed subsequently), it is generally accepted that BOLD reflects broad spectrum LFP fluctuations more than spiking output, although this finding may be at times over-simplified. Therefore I suggest a brief discussion of this issue either in the Materials and methods (to justify the choice) or the Discussion (to acknowledge a partial limitation).

The reviewers' points are provided in full (because they are detailed and constructive), but where possible we will endeavour to rely on editorial discretion in appraising the revisions.

Reviewer #1:

In this work, the authors first demonstrated an association between E/I balance and Hurst component (H) by showing that [1] in a computational study, the Hurst component based on LFP was positively correlated with E/I balance, [2] also in-silico, the H based on BOLD signals was positively correlated with E/I balance –this part is predictable given prior work about the LFP-BOLD association – and [3] in vivo, the BOLD-based H was increased when neuronal excitability was enhanced.

Afterwards, they showed [4] MPFC was among human brain regions whose gene expression had both male-specific and autism-specific patterns, [5] in resting-state fMRI signals, a significant sex-diagnosis interaction effect was found in Hurst component in vMPFC and [6] only in the autistic female, the H was correlated with the camouflaging score.

Based on these observations, the authors claim that [A] Hurst component can be an index for the E/I balance and [B] the association between E/I balance and autism differs between sexes.

The theme (E/I balance, autism and sex difference) is important and each observation appears scientifically sound. In particular, the first half about the relationship between E/I balance and H (results [1]-[3] in above) is straight forward and looks solid. Relatively, the last half could be improved if the following concerns are addressed.

First, I think readers would like to know the spatial relationship between the MPFC found in the gene analysis and the vMPFC detected in the following rsfMRI analysis. In my understanding, if the authors want to say any link between sex-related genes and autism/sex-specific H changes, these two regions should be somewhat overlapped.

Second, I think readers would appreciate it if the authors supply some more information about associations between Hurst component in the vMFPC and behaviours/symptoms: at least, in both sexes, associations between H and symptom severity (total, social part and RRB component, respectively) in autistic individuals and those between H and AQ scores in both TD and autistic groups in both sexes. Such additional information would be quite helpful to re-interpret the function of the brain area in each sex and in TD and autism.

Reviewer #2:

In this study, Trakoshis, Martinez-Cañada and colleagues take a multi-scale approach to study how altered excitation-inhibition balance manifests in spectral features of the fMRI BOLD signal and apply it to study autism. Combining computational modeling of recurrent spiking neural networks, rodent chemogenetic experiments in-vivo, and sex- and autism-related gene expression in neuronal stem cells and post-mortem brain tissue, the authors relate changes in Hurst exponent (H) and 1/f exponent of the power spectrum to modulation of neuronal excitation specifically. With this link, they argue for a mechanistic interpretation of BOLD signal differences (in H) between autistic males and females, as well as the neural correlate of social camouflaging in females only.

The study is well-designed and logically presented, and I especially commend the multiscale approach that start with computational modeling to establish experimental hypotheses. Overall, I believe the paper is of quality and within the scope of eLife, as it integrates several levels of biology and thus appeals to a broad audience. Substantive concerns regarding modeling and analysis choices, as well as potentially problematic interpretations are listed below. I would recommend the manuscript for publication after those are addressed through additional analyses and writing changes, without collection of additional data.

Major comments:

1) I have two potential issues regarding the simulation of BOLD from LFP. First – and I do not claim domain expertise here whatsoever – it seems to me that BOLD should be simulated by convolving the HRF with the spiking output of the circuit, not the LFP. The LFP, as the authors note, is a combination of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic fluctuations. While taking the summation of the absolute value of those fluctuations will approximate local spiking, the latter is a true representation of the circuit's output, and is less affected by the strength of the inputs.

2) Second, and related, is that the authors draw attention to the frequency-dependent correlation between BOLD and LFP power, as correlation increases with frequency. But this pattern in correlation is essentially baked into the model itself, since a high-pass filter is applied after convolution with the HRF, imposing a higher correlation in higher frequencies. In addition, while this model partially recapitulates empirical data, it's also been shown that there is a negative correlation between LFP low-frequency power (e.g., α, 8-12 Hz) and BOLD (e.g., Mukamel et al., 2005). While it's good that the authors demonstrate changes in H to be unaltered by a conventional HRF-convolution model, I would like them to please comment on these two points, and whether the latter can be recapitulated in their model. If not, this is a good point of limitation to discuss.

3) When simulating the effect of DREADD silencing, do the neurons still spike at very low leak potentials? If not, then the LFP is effectively driven by the statistics of the cortical and thalamic inputs, which would represent a different circuit regime from the recurrent interactions enabled by higher leak potentials. While this does not change the conclusion of the study drastically, it would implicate the non-recurrent inputs to be the key factor in shaping H in this instance, which can alter the interpretation of the DREADD data.

4) A related point: the spiking network model represents some local circuit that receives cortical inputs. When simulating the effect of DREADD, only EL is changed, but not the cortical inputs. How realistic is this assumption? In other words, how local is the effect of DREADD on the resting state activity in the PFC? Additionally, while the authors show changes in H (or the lack thereof) in the two DREADD experiments, does absolute amplitude of BOLD fluctuations change in the expected directions, e.g., an increase with excitation and decrease with silencing?

5) The rat is anesthetized prior to chemogenetic manipulation, which already shifts E:I balance. Without collecting data from pre-anesthesia periods, it's hard to say what those changes in H are, and how they compare relative to the DREADD manipulation. But the authors should at least discuss this point, and I would even suggest trying to simulate the additional effect of anesthesia to see if there is an interaction with DREADD (though this is not necessary).

6) E:I is interpreted to be normal in autistic females (no difference in H between TD and ASD females), but there is significant covariation with behavior, which is one of the main findings of the study. However, this begs the question: how much variation in H can be attributed to "healthy behavior-modulated variation", and how much to pathology? In Figure 5B, it looks like the range in H in the female autism cohort straddles the TD and ASD male cohorts, with comparable standard deviation. On the other hand, H does not correlate with the degree of social camouflaging in the male ASD cohort, yet there is still significant variation in the amount of camouflaging they are capable of. Is there a separate mechanism at play for camouflaging in males then? How do the authors settle these two seemingly contradictory findings?

7) Subsection “Human fMRI data analysis” appears to state that the mean of the BOLD timeseries across voxel is taken first, from which H is computed. Doesn't it make more sense to compute H for each voxel and then average after? How different are these two situations? I don't have an intuition for how averaging timeseries affect H, but an analogous situation in spectral analysis is destructive interference, where two high-amplitude oscillations may combine to a flat signal due to a phase difference.

8) Another method question: why not fit PLS directly with the 2-column matrix (CF1 and CF2) directly, since PLS is capable of outputting a single explanatory component, instead of performing PCA first. They should be similar?

9) Similarly (and maybe I'm not understanding something here), why not fit PLS or mass univariate over the entire cortex for camouflaging as well, as the authors did to find spatial specificity for the sex*diagnosis contrast, instead of only regressing in vMPFC specifically?

10) Lastly, while I appreciate the ample reference to Gao et al., 2017, I suggest the authors check out Lombardi et al., 2017 as well, as they also look at how 1/f changes as a result of E:I shifts, but with a recurrent and interacting-E:I spiking model that is arguably more similar to the model in this manuscript. However, their finding is in contrast to Gao et al., 2017, where 1/f flattens for increasing inhibition. This is worth referencing and noting in the discussions.

Reviewer #3:

This is an impressive piece of work combining multi-level methods and different modalities using both mouse and human data that substantially enhances our understanding of E:I imbalance in autism. The authors demonstrate and extend the link between E:I balance and the Hurst component and 1/f slope in local field potentials and rsfMRI data using a biologically more plausible network model than prior work. They further establish the spatial distribution of autism-linked genes associated with excitation and androgen-sensitive genes that coincide with the sex-differential region associated with the H-component in the human rsfMRI data. Interestingly, this region also shows a sex-differential relationship to camouflaging behavior. This is an impressive set of analyses with elaborate and thorough methodological steps. Listed below are some minor comments that can help increase the clarity of the manuscript and interpretation of the results.

1) The authors start the Introduction with the sentence that E:I imbalance affects many disorders. This calls for at least a short mention in the Discussion how findings are specific to autism.

2) The Introduction lacks a bit of a red line to my taste. It would be clearer to read if sub-paragraphs were linked to each other. The different sections make sense – however it is left to the reader to link them to each other. Given the complexity and many aspects touched on, I think the flow of the Introduction could still be improved a bit.

3) Could authors explain in more details what “in silico” refers to in this context? This might not be clear to a broad readership.

4) How was mean frame-wise displacement calculated? Power? Jenkinson?

5) In Table 3, could authors also report differences in symptom scores and camouflaging between autistic males and females.

6) What is the justification for the use of PLS on top? What additional information is revealed?

7) A large part of the results is in mouse data. The Introduction should thus also include a section introducing how E:I imbalance can be investigated in animal models. Right now, the Introduction refers solely to human participants, whereas the entire first Result section does not.

8) Given the results first format, it should be pointed out briefly which dataset was used for which set of results. The first section should clearly state that this is done in the mouse data for example.

9) The sex-differential results in humans are intriguing. However, when looking at Figure 5B, I wonder whether a gender-incoherent pattern is evident here? Could authors further discuss this? Also, in line with this, I wonder whether authors could refine this part of the Discussion stating: "Thus, one potential explanation for the male-specific reduction of H in vMPFC could have to do with early developmental and androgen-sensitive upregulation of genes that play central roles in excitatory neuron cell types, and thus ultimately affecting downstream E:I imbalance. Such effects may be sex-differential and thus less critical in human females, serving an important basis of sex-differential human brain development and explaining the sex-based heterogeneity and qualitative sex differences of autism neurobiology in human." Do authors refer to typical females here? The results look like TD females show a similar pattern to autistic males. So how do authors explain the differential pattern in TD females and autistic females.

10) I like the link to the camouflaging behavior. However, the question arises whether there is also a sex-differential link to core autistic symptoms such as for example repetitive behaviors that have also been shown to differ across autistic males and females?

11) Could authors include information on the age range of autistic subjects (currently, I can't see the age range anywhere) and discuss the potential effect of age on their results from a neurodevelopmental perspective?

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: In the recurrent network model, as E:I ratio increases (by decreasing g), H decreases, but only when g is below the baseline reference value.
claims.source: As expected, H decreases with decreasing g (i.e. increasing E:I ratio), but only when g is below the baseline reference value (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: In the recurrent network model, changes in synaptic E:I ratio are reflected by and could be inferred from the overall LFP readout of 1/f slope or H.
claims.source: These results clearly indicate that, in a biologically plausible computational model of local cortical microcircuitry including recurrent connections between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations, changes in synaptic E:I ratio are reflected by and thus could be inferred from the overall LFP readout of 1/f slope or H.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claims.claim: Simulated BOLD from the recurrent model shows that H in BOLD decreases as E:I ratio is shifted toward higher excitation by lowering the value of g with respect to the reference value.
claims.source: Strikingly, H in BOLD shows the same dependency on g as observed in LFP data (Figure 2C-D) - H in BOLD decreases as E:I ratio is shifted toward higher excitation by lowering the value of g with respect to the reference value.
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: Studies with simultaneous LFP and BOLD measured in animals have shown that BOLD signal correlates more strongly with the LFP than with spikes.
claims.source: Studies with simultaneous LFP and BOLD measured in animals have shown that although BOLD signal correlates with both LFPs and spikes, it correlates more strongly with the LFP than with spikes (Logothetis et al., 2001; Magri et al., 2012; Rauch et al., 2008; Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007; Lauritzen and Gold, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior empirical work.

claims.claim: LFP power shows time-lagged correlations with the time course of BOLD signal and different frequency bands vary in how they correlate with measured BOLD signal.
claims.source: Further studies with simultaneous LFP and BOLD measured in non-human primates (Logothetis et al., 2001; Magri et al., 2012; Schölvinck et al., 2010) have considered the relationship between frequency-resolved LFPs and BOLD and indicate that LFP power shows time-lagged correlations with the time course of BOLD signal and that different frequency bands vary in how they correlate with measured BOLD signal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claims.claim: Gamma band frequencies tend to show the strongest correlation between LFP power and BOLD signal.
claims.source: In particular, gamma band frequencies tend to show the strongest correlation between LFP power and BOLD signal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claims.claim: Frequency dependency of the EEG-BOLD relationship, with prominent predictive power of the gamma band, is reported in humans.
claims.source: Frequency dependency of the EEG-BOLD relationship, with prominent predictive power of the gamma band, is also reported in humans (Scheeringa et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The method for simulating BOLD from recurrent model LFP data retains key empirical relationships observed between real LFP power and BOLD.
claims.source: Thus, our method for simulating BOLD from recurrent model LFP data retains key empirical relationships observed between real LFP power and BOLD.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulated data to empirical observations.

claims.claim: In the recurrent model simulation of hM3Dq DREADD manipulation, progressively lowering voltage threshold for spike initiation from -52 to -53 mV resulted in more positive low-frequency and flatter high-frequency 1/f slopes and caused decreases in H.
claims.source: Progressively lowering Vth from -52 to -53 mV resulted in more positive low-frequency and flatter high-frequency 1/f slopes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and also caused decreases in H (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In the recurrent model simulation of hM4Di DREADD manipulation, decreasing the resting potential from -70 to -75 mV produced varied effects in 1/f slopes and resulted in a slight increase of H.
claims.source: Decreasing EL from the baseline value of -70 to -75 mV produced varied effects in 1/f slopes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and resulted in a slight increase of H (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In mouse PFC, H is modulated over time by the hM3Dq DREADD excitation manipulation.
claims.source: We find that H is modulated over time by the DREADD manipulation (condition*time*treatment phase interaction F = 349.03, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data.

claims.claim: During the Baseline phase of rsfMRI scanning before the DREADD-actuator CNO was injected, H under DREADD or a SHAM control conditions are not affected.
claims.source: During the Baseline phase of rsfMRI scanning before the DREADD-actuator CNO was injected, H under DREADD or a SHAM control conditions are not affected (condition main effect F = 0.82, p=0.37; condition*time interaction F = 0.36, p=0.54).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data.

claims.claim: During the Transition phase of the hM3Dq DREADD experiment, H drops over time at a steeper rate during the DREADD condition compared to the SHAM condition.
claims.source: However, during the Transition phase of the experiment where the CNO begins to have its effects, we find a condition*time interaction (F = 4.94, p=0.0262), whereby H drops over time at a steeper rate during the DREADD condition compared to the SHAM condition (green line in Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: During the Treatment phase of the hM3Dq DREADD experiment, H is reduced in the DREADD vs SHAM condition.
claims.source: Finally, during the Treatment phase of the experiment, where the drug exerts its maximal effect, there is a significant main effect of condition (F = 12.92, p=0.0011) and no condition*time interaction (F = 0.66, p=0.4182) (blue line in Figure 3C) (Table 1). This effect is explained by H being reduced in the DREADD vs SHAM condition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claims.claim: Chemogenetically silencing both excitatory and inhibitory neurons with hM4Di DREADD has no strong main effects of condition or condition*time interactions in any of the baseline, transition, or treatment phases of the experiment.
claims.source: While a significant 3-way interaction between condition, time, and treatment phase was present (F = 85.8, p<0.0001), there were no strong main effects of condition or condition*time interactions in any of the baseline, transition, or treatment phases of the experiment (see Table 2 and Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data shown in Figure 3D and Table 2.

claims.claim: Genes differentially expressed by DHT are highly prominent within the gene set of autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neurons (OR = 1.67, p=0.03).
claims.source: Genes differentially expressed by DHT are highly prominent within the gene set of autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neurons (OR = 1.67, p=0.03), with most of the overlapping genes being those whereby DHT upregulates expression (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: Genes associated with autism that affect inhibitory neuronal cell types or other non-neuronal cells (e.g., microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes) are not enriched for DHT differentially expressed genes.
claims.source: By contrast, genes associated with autism that affect inhibitory neuronal cell types or other non-neuronal cells (e.g., microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes) are not enriched for DHT differentially expressed genes (inhibitory neurons: OR = 1.51, p=0.12; microglia: OR = 0.78, p=0.78; astrocytes or oligodendrocytes: OR = 1.11, p=0.49).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data.

claims.claim: DHT-sensitive and autism-associated excitatory neuron genes are highly expressed in MPFC, PCC, insula, and intraparietal sulcus in the adult human brain.
claims.source: A one-sample t-test of gene maps from the Allen Institute Human Brain Atlas (Hawrylycz et al., 2012) shows that this subset of DHT-sensitive and autism-associated excitatory neuron genes are highly expressed in MPFC, PCC, insula, and intraparietal sulcus, amongst other areas (Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4B-C.

claims.claim: Mass-univariate analysis uncovered one region in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vMPFC), region p32, with a sex-by-diagnosis interaction passing FDR q < 0.05 (F(5,104) = 15.13, p=0.0001, partial η2 = 0.12).
claims.source: Mass-univariate analysis uncovered one region in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vMPFC), region p32, with a sex-by-diagnosis interaction passing FDR q < 0.05 (F(5,104) = 15.13, p=0.0001, partial η2 = 0.12) (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: The sex-by-diagnosis interaction in vMPFC area p32 is driven by a large TD >Autism effect in males (Cohen's d = 1.30) and a small Autism >TD effect in females (Cohen's d = −0.27).
claims.source: In line with directionality of our predictions, this interaction effect is driven by a large TD >Autism effect in males (Cohen's d = 1.30) and a small Autism >TD effect in females (Cohen's d = −0.27) (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by effect size analysis of human rsfMRI data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: PLS analysis identified one neural system expressing the sex-by-diagnosis interaction (d = 2.04, p=0.036) that included default mode network (DMN) areas such as MPFC and posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus (PCC).
claims.source: PLS analysis identified one neural system expressing the same sex-by-diagnosis interaction (d = 2.04, p=0.036) and included default mode network (DMN) areas such as MPFC and posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus (PCC) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and other non-DMN areas such as insula, lateral prefrontal cortex, somatosensory and motor cortices, intraparietal sulcus, amongst others (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PLS analysis of human rsfMRI data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In autistic females, increased camouflaging was strongly associated with increased H in vMPFC (r = 0.60, p=0.001).
claims.source: In autistic females, increased camouflaging was strongly associated with increased H in vMPFC (r = 0.60, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and behavioral data.

claims.claim: In autistic males, there is no significant association between camouflaging and H in vMPFC (r = −0.10, p=0.63).
claims.source: However, no significant association was apparent in autistic males (r = −0.10, p=0.63).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and behavioral data.

claims.claim: The strength of the brain-behavioral correlation between H and camouflaging significantly differed between autistic males and females (z = 2.58, p=0.009).
claims.source: The strength of this brain-behavioral correlation significantly differed between autistic males and females (z = 2.58, p=0.009) (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of correlations shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: ADOS social-communication (SC) was negatively correlated with vMPFC H in autistic females (r = −0.51, p=0.008) indicating higher H with lower SC severity.
claims.source: ADOS social-communication (SC) was negatively correlated with vMPFC H in autistic females (r = −0.51, p=0.008) indicating higher H with lower SC severity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and clinical data.

claims.claim: The relationship between ADOS social-communication and vMPFC H was not present in autistic males (r = −0.04, p=0.83).
claims.source: This relationship was not present in autistic males (r = −0.04, p=0.83).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and clinical data.

claims.claim: The recurrent network model includes interactions within and between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations.
claims.source: Importantly, our approach takes a major step forward from prior work (Gao et al., 2017) by utilizing a model that includes interactions within and between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the computational model used in the study.

claims.claim: The recurrent network model is composed of 5000 neurons, of which 4000 are excitatory and 1000 inhibitory.
claims.source: The network is composed of 5000 neurons, of which 4000 are excitatory (i.e. they form AMPA-like excitatory synapses with other neurons) and 1000 inhibitory (forming GABA-like synapses).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters.

claims.claim: In the recurrent network model, neurons are randomly connected with a connection probability between each pair of neurons of 0.2.
claims.source: Neurons are randomly connected with a connection probability between each pair of neurons of 0.2.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters.

claims.claim: The LFP in the recurrent model is computed as the sum of absolute values of AMPA and GABA postsynaptic currents on excitatory cells.
claims.source: The LFP is computed as the sum of absolute values of AMPA and GABA postsynaptic currents on excitatory cells (Mazzoni et al., 2008; Mazzoni et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the computational method with citation support.

claims.claim: The simple estimation of LFPs was shown to capture more than 90% of variance of both experimental data recorded from cortical field potentials and of simulated data from a complex three-dimensional model of the dipoles generated by cortical neurons.
claims.source: This simple estimation of LFPs was shown to capture more than 90% of variance of both experimental data recorded from cortical field potentials and of simulated data from a complex three-dimensional model of the dipoles generated by cortical neurons (Mazzoni et al., 2008; Mazzoni et al., 2015; Barbieri et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior validation work.

claims.claim: The relationship between E:I and the spectral slope flattens out for high values of I in the recurrent model.
claims.source: In contrast, we found that the relationship between E:I and the spectral slope flattens out for high values of I.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling results.

claims.claim: Higher recurrent inhibition leads to higher peak frequency of gamma oscillations.
claims.source: This, in our view, may in part arise from the fact that, as shown in studies of recurrent network models (Brunel and Wang, 2003), higher recurrent inhibition leads to higher peak frequency of gamma oscillations (i.e. an increase of power at higher frequencies) thus partly counteracting the low-pass filtering effect of inhibitory currents in the uncoupled model.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior work and current modeling results.

claims.claim: The model to generate BOLD from frequency-resolved LFPs reflects several features of the empirical LFP-BOLD relationship - namely the presence of a particularly strong gamma-BOLD relationship and the fact that a better prediction of the BOLD is obtained from the frequency-resolved LFP than from the wideband LFP.
claims.source: Our simple model to generate BOLD from frequency-resolved LFPs reflect several features of the empirical LFP-BOLD relationship - namely the presence of a particularly strong gamma-BOLD relationship and the fact that a better prediction of the BOLD is obtained from the frequency-resolved LFP than from the wideband LFP.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the computational model's properties.

claims.claim: A limitation of the simple model is that it cannot capture the negative relationship between the power of some low-frequency LFP bands and the BOLD amplitude that has been reported in some studies.
claims.source: However, a limitation of our simple model is that, in its present form, it cannot capture the negative relationship between the power of some low-frequency LFP bands and the BOLD amplitude that has been reported in some studies (Schölvinck et al., 2010; Scheeringa et al., 2011; Mukamel et al., 2005; Niessing et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the computational model.

claims.claim: Enhancement of excitation in mouse MPFC results in measurable changes in BOLD readouts as decreases in H.
claims.source: The present work clearly shows that enhancement of excitation results in measurable changes in BOLD readouts as decreases in H.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in-vivo mouse experiments.

claims.claim: Autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neuronal cell types are enriched for genes that are differentially expressed by DHT in human neuronal stem cells.
claims.source: With regards to how sex-related heterogeneity in E:I imbalance might manifest in autism, we utilized genomics data and found that autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neuronal cell types are enriched for genes that are differentially expressed by DHT in human neuronal stem cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data.

claims.claim: Other cell types such as inhibitory neurons do not express autism-associated genes that are also influenced by DHT.
claims.source: Importantly, other cell types such as inhibitory neurons do not express autism-associated genes that are also influenced by DHT.
claims.evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data.

claims.claim: Reduced H in autistic males is compatible with the inference of elevated E:I ratio potentially driven by enhanced excitation.
claims.source: Specifically, we examined whether H differs between adult males and females with and without autism. Mass-univariate analysis highlighted one region in vMPFC which showed a sex-by-diagnosis interaction - that is, H was specifically reduced in adult autistic males, but not in autistic females. Reduced H in autistic males is compatible with the inference of elevated E:I ratio potentially driven by enhanced excitation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the human rsfMRI results in the context of the modeling and mouse experiments.

claims.claim: Progressively more intact vMPFC H in autistic females, which are likely reflective of more intact E:I balance, is associated with better ability to camouflage social-communicative difficulties.
claims.source: Strikingly, here we find a similar sex-by-diagnosis interaction effect in vMPFC H as well as a female-specific correlation with camouflaging - as vMPFC H increases, indicative of a more normative or intact level of E:I balance, camouflaging also increases. This converging set of results suggests that intrinsic mechanisms such as E:I balance may be atypical only in cognitively able autistic males at vMPFC. More intact E:I balance in the vMPFC of autistic females may enable better vMPFC-related function (e.g., self-representation) and thus potentially better enable these individuals to camouflage social-communicative difficulties and cope in social situations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis between H and camouflaging in autistic females.

claims.claim: Intact E:I balance in vMPFC of females may be an expression of protective factors that are hypothesized to buffer risk for autism in females.
claims.source: It may also be fruitful to examine how intact E:I balance in vMPFC of females may be an expression of protective factors that are hypothesized to buffer risk for autism in females (Robinson et al., 2013; Werling, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings, supported by citations to prior work on protective factors.

claims.claim: Spectral properties of neural time-series data, such as H and 1/f slope, can be utilized in neuroimaging readouts like LFP and BOLD as a biomarker for underlying E:I-relevant mechanisms.
claims.source: In conclusion, we show that spectral properties of neural time-series data, such as H and 1/f slope, can be utilized in neuroimaging readouts like LFP and BOLD as a biomarker for underlying E:I-relevant mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in-silico, in-vivo, and human data.

claims.claim: H in rsfMRI data is reduced in vMPFC and other DMN areas of adult autistic males, but not females.
claims.source: Finally, in application to humans, we show that H in rsfMRI data is reduced in vMPFC and other DMN areas of adult autistic males, but not females.
claims.evidence: This is supported by human rsfMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Reduced H is indicative of enhanced excitation and thus points to sex-specific dysregulation of E:I balance in social brain networks of autistic males.
claims.source: Reduced H is indicative of enhanced excitation and thus points to sex-specific dysregulation of E:I balance in social brain networks of autistic males.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the human rsfMRI results in the context of the modeling and mouse experiments.

claims.claim: Male-specific dysregulation of E:I balance may be linked to sex-differential early developmental events such as androgen-upregulation of gene expression for genes that play important roles in excitatory neurons.
claims.source: This male-specific dysregulation of E:I balance may be linked to sex-differential early developmental events such as androgen-upregulation of gene expression for genes that play important roles in excitatory neurons (Lombardo et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the developmental mechanisms, supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The intact levels of H in females may help facilitate elevated levels of compensation known as camouflaging to cope with daily social-communicative difficulties.
claims.source: The intact levels of H in females may help facilitate elevated levels of compensation known as camouflaging to cope with daily social-communicative difficulties.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between H and camouflaging in autistic females.

claims.claim: This work extends the relevance of the E:I imbalance theory of autism beyond evidence from autism-associated rare genetic variants and specify a larger portion of the autism population whereby these E:I mechanisms may be of critical importance.
claims.source: More generally, this work extends the relevance of the E:I imbalance theory of autism beyond evidence from autism-associated rare genetic variants and specify a larger portion of the autism population whereby these E:I mechanisms may be of critical importance.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the work.

claims.claim: When H > 1 the time-series is considered non-stationary and has long memory characteristics (e.g., is fractal).

results.result: In a recurrent network model of interacting excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations, changes in synaptic E:I ratio are reflected by changes in 1/f slope and Hurst exponent (H) in simulated LFP data. Specifically, H decreases when E:I ratio increases (by decreasing g below baseline), but only in the excitation-dominated regime.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 and C48-C54 collectively describe the recurrent network model architecture and demonstrate through computational simulations that H and 1/f slope track with E:I ratio changes. The model includes biologically plausible features (5000 neurons, recurrent connections, validated LFP computation methods) and shows clear relationships between g (inhibitory/excitatory conductance ratio) and spectral properties. The results are internally consistent and supported by figures showing the dose-response relationships.

results.result: Simulated BOLD signal from the recurrent model shows that H in BOLD decreases as E:I ratio increases, mirroring the relationship observed in LFP data. The BOLD simulation method captures key empirical relationships between LFP power and BOLD, particularly the strong gamma-band correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 and C55-C56 demonstrate that the LFP-to-BOLD transformation preserves the E:I-H relationship and recapitulates known empirical features (gamma-band dominance, frequency-dependent correlations). The method is described in detail (C93-C94) and validated against prior empirical observations (C25-C28). However, C56 acknowledges a limitation regarding low-frequency negative correlations, which is appropriately transparent.

results.result: In silico simulations of DREADD manipulations predict that lowering voltage threshold (simulating hM3Dq excitation) decreases H, while decreasing resting potential (simulating hM4Di silencing) produces minimal effects on H.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 describe computational predictions for specific experimental manipulations. The results show clear directional effects for excitation enhancement (decreased H) and minimal effects for pan-neuronal silencing, providing testable predictions. These are supported by supplementary figures showing 1/f slope changes across parameter ranges.

results.result: Chemogenetic enhancement of excitation (hM3Dq DREADD) in mouse prefrontal cortex causes a significant decrease in H during the treatment phase, confirming in silico predictions. This effect is specific to excitation enhancement, as evidenced by appropriate baseline controls and temporal dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 present in vivo validation with appropriate statistical analysis (3-way interactions, phase-specific effects) and controls (baseline, SHAM conditions). The temporal dynamics (no baseline effect, transition interaction, treatment main effect) are consistent with drug pharmacokinetics. Supporting claims C86-C91 provide methodological details and convergent evidence from fALFF analysis. The results directly confirm the in silico predictions from C30.

results.result: Chemogenetic silencing of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (hM4Di DREADD) shows no strong effects on H across experimental phases, serving as a negative control that strengthens the interpretation that decreased H specifically reflects increased excitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C87 demonstrate appropriate negative control results with statistical analysis showing no main effects or interactions in individual phases, despite a 3-way interaction. This is consistent with in silico predictions (C31) and strengthens the specificity of the excitation findings. The fALFF data (C87) provides convergent evidence.

results.result: Autism-associated genes affecting excitatory neurons are significantly enriched for genes differentially expressed by dihydrotestosterone (DHT) (OR=1.67, p=0.03), while genes affecting inhibitory neurons or other cell types show no such enrichment. This suggests sex-specific androgen effects on excitatory neuron biology may contribute to E:I imbalance in autism.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 and C58-C59 present genomic enrichment analysis with appropriate statistical testing (odds ratios, hypergeometric p-values) and proper background correction (C97). The cell-type specificity (excitatory but not inhibitory neurons) strengthens the interpretation. The methodology is clearly described (C96) and the results are internally consistent.

results.result: DHT-sensitive autism-associated excitatory neuron genes are highly expressed in MPFC, PCC, insula, and intraparietal sulcus in the adult human brain, with substantial overlap (59-85%) with brain regions showing sex-by-diagnosis interactions in H.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C81-C83 demonstrate spatial convergence between genomic and neuroimaging findings. The gene expression analysis uses established methods (Allen Brain Atlas, one-sample t-test, FDR correction) and the overlap analysis provides quantitative estimates. This convergence strengthens the mechanistic interpretation linking androgen-sensitive genes to regional E:I effects.

results.result: In human rsfMRI data, ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vMPFC area p32) shows a significant sex-by-diagnosis interaction in H (F=15.13, p=0.0001, partial η²=0.12), driven by reduced H in autistic males (Cohen's d=1.30) but not females (d=-0.27). Groups were well-matched on age, IQ, and head motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 present the primary human neuroimaging finding with appropriate statistics (FDR correction, effect sizes) and directional consistency with predictions. Claims C70-C75 and C79 demonstrate adequate control for confounds (age, IQ, motion) and appropriate multiple comparison correction. The large effect size in males and specificity to one region after correction suggests a robust, localized effect.

results.result: Multivariate PLS analysis identified a distributed neural system including default mode network areas (MPFC, PCC) and other regions (insula, intraparietal sulcus) expressing the sex-by-diagnosis interaction (d=2.04, p=0.036). Additionally, 61% of brain regions showed male>female sex differences in H.
results.evaluation: Claims C42 and C80 extend the mass-univariate findings using appropriate multivariate methods with permutation testing and bootstrap resampling. The PLS results are consistent with the univariate findings and the genomic expression patterns. The sex difference finding (C80) provides normative context, though the manuscript notes that sex-specific norms need better establishment in larger datasets.

results.result: In autistic females, higher vMPFC H is strongly associated with increased camouflaging ability (r=0.60, p=0.001), while no such relationship exists in autistic males (r=-0.10, p=0.63). The correlation strength significantly differs between sexes (z=2.58, p=0.009), suggesting that more intact E:I balance in vMPFC may facilitate compensatory behaviors in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 present a sex-specific brain-behavior relationship with appropriate statistical testing (correlations, Fisher's z-test). The camouflaging measure is operationalized consistently with prior work (C84-C85) using validated methods (PCA of multiple indices). The finding converges with prior task-fMRI work on vMPFC self-representation and provides a functional interpretation of the sex-specific H differences.

results.result: ADOS social-communication severity is negatively correlated with vMPFC H in autistic females (r=-0.51, p=0.008) but not males (r=-0.04, p=0.83), though the difference between correlations does not reach significance (z=1.70, p=0.08).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 present an exploratory clinical correlation that shows a pattern consistent with the camouflaging findings but fails to reach significance for the between-group comparison. While the within-female correlation is significant, the lack of significant sex difference limits the strength of inference. This appears to be an exploratory analysis rather than a primary hypothesis-driven test.

results.result: The Hurst exponent (H) estimated from fMRI BOLD signal can serve as a biomarker for underlying synaptic E:I ratio, extending the relevance of E:I imbalance theory beyond rare genetic variants to a larger portion of the autism population.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C63, and C68 represent the overarching conclusions synthesizing the in silico, in vivo, and human findings. The multi-level validation (computational modeling, mouse experiments, human neuroimaging) provides strong convergent evidence. However, the biomarker claim should be interpreted cautiously as it relies on indirect inference through multiple transformation steps (synaptic activity→LFP→BOLD→H) and has only been validated for one direction of manipulation (increased excitation).

results.result: The manuscript establishes theoretical and empirical background regarding E:I imbalance in autism, sex differences in autism prevalence, the influence of sex-related mechanisms on E:I balance, spectral properties of neural signals, and prior work on H in autism and camouflaging in autistic females.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C21 represent background knowledge and prior work that is appropriately cited and provides context for the current study. These claims are supported by citations to established literature and represent accurate characterizations of the field. They establish the rationale for investigating sex-specific E:I imbalance using spectral biomarkers.

results.result: The human participants were cis-gender, and the fMRI preprocessing used wavelet denoising to control motion artifacts. The Hurst exponent was estimated using a fractionally integrated process (FIP) model with discrete wavelet transform and maximum likelihood estimation, which offers advantages over prior fractional Gaussian noise models.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C73-C78 describe important methodological details. The participant characterization (C69) is appropriate for the study design. The preprocessing method (C73) is validated by prior work. The H estimation method (C76-C78) is clearly described with appropriate justification for methodological choices. These are standard methodological details that support the validity of the analyses.

results.result: The authors speculate that intact E:I balance in vMPFC of females may represent protective factors buffering autism risk, and that male-specific E:I dysregulation may be linked to early developmental androgen effects on excitatory neuron gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C66 represent speculative interpretations about developmental mechanisms and protective factors. While these are plausible hypotheses consistent with the data and cited literature, they are explicitly framed as speculation and future directions rather than demonstrated findings. The developmental timing and causal mechanisms remain to be tested.
